name: Brow lamination kit

lead: A brow lamination kit uses chemical solutions to relax the bonds in brow hairs so they can be brushed up and outward and set in a fluffy, uniform direction. Users want fuller-looking, brushed-up brows, with results lasting about four to six weeks.

It works like a perm: a reducing agent breaks disulfide bonds in hair keratin, then a neutralizer re-forms them in the new position. It is sold as a salon service and as home kits. A 2025 review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology states it is the first to address side effects of brow lamination.

paras: Users apply the lifting solution, brush brows upward, then apply the neutralizer, often followed by tinting or a conditioning serum. The result is redone every four to six weeks. Salon treatment is common, and DIY kits copy the process.

Over-processing can leave hairs dry and brittle, and chemicals near the eyes can cause irritation, allergic reaction or chemical injury. Experts advise patch testing and have said at-home use carries more risk than professional application. No controlled trials of outcomes were identified.

What Is Brow Lamination & Is It The New Microblading?

angle.text: Users apply perm-like solutions to brows to set them brushed up and uniform, giving a fuller, fluffier look said to last about four to six weeks. The chemicals relax and re-form hair bonds so the new direction holds. A 2025 review calls for more study of its side effects.

lead: A brow lamination kit is a set of chemical solutions that relaxes the keratin bonds in eyebrow hairs so they can be brushed upward and outward and held in a uniform, fluffy direction. The process is comparable to a hair perm. Lamination is sold as a salon service and as at-home kits, and people use it to make brows look fuller, thicker, more groomed and more defined without makeup, microblading or a transplant [1][2].

Results are commonly described as lasting several weeks: sources give different ranges: two to six weeks (New Beauty) [2], six to eight weeks (Medical News Today, matching the usual brow growth cycle) [1], and about eight weeks (Nylon) [3]. In salons the service is often combined with tinting. Brow artist Niki Metz described it in 2020 as "similar to microblading but without the needle and longevity" [3].

A 2025 review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology states it is the first to address possible side effects of brow lamination, and it calls for more studies and regulation [4]. No controlled trials of lamination outcomes were identified, and eye-care commentary describes comparable risks from related lash perms and tints [5].
infobox: $15-30 for a kit; roughly $50-120 for a salon session [1]

paras: A kit generally contains a lifting (reducing) lotion, a setting (neutralizing) lotion, a nourishing oil or serum and applicators. The brow hairs are brushed into the desired direction, treated with each solution in sequence and cleaned. Brow lamination is often combined with tinting in salons.

Medical News Today describes the salon sequence as a patch test, cleaning and marking the brow shape, application of a keratin-infused lifting cream while the hairs are brushed upward and covered, removal and application of a setting solution, and finishing with an oil or serum; the visit takes about 45 to 60 minutes and costs around $50 to $120 depending on provider and location [1].

Nylon reported in January 2020 that brow lamination originated in Russia about three years earlier and had become a salon trend promoted by beauty editors and influencers, comparing it to a Brazilian blowout for brows [3]. It adapts the chemistry used for permanent waves and lash lifts: an aesthetician quoted by New Beauty calls it a "reverse perm" for brows [2]. Beauty media presents it as part of a shift toward fuller, natural-looking brows after the thin, heavily plucked shapes of the 1920s and 1930s and the rise of cosmetic tattooing and microblading in the 21st century [6][3]. The 2025 Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology review describes brow lamination as an emerging technique that is widely used [4].

Hair keratin is held in shape by disulfide bonds. A reducing agent, commonly a thioglycolate such as ammonium thioglycolate, breaks the bonds so the hair can be repositioned, and a neutralizer re-forms them in the new arrangement [4].
Eyebrow hair is short and has a brief growth phase, and reference sources describe a growth cycle of about three to four months, which relates to how long a new shape persists as hairs shed [7].

Medical News Today describes lamination as suited to people with thin, curly or unruly brow hair that grows in different directions, uneven brows, gaps from overplucking or overwaxing, and thinning with age or illness. It lists sensitive skin, eczema, contact dermatitis, rosacea and chemical allergies as reasons to avoid it or speak to a dermatologist first. [1] New Beauty describes it as for people whose brows do not hold their shape with clear brow gel. [2]

Practitioners quoted in beauty media suggest keeping the brows dry and free of makeup and skincare products for the first 24 hours. Medical News Today suggests avoiding retinol-type exfoliants for 72 hours and conditioning the brows with oil or serum, while a New Beauty aesthetician suggests three to five days without exfoliants and retinoids. [1][2] Both articles caution against frequent repeats: Medical News Today advises against more than one treatment within six weeks, and brow specialist Joey Healy tells New Beauty to use lamination sparingly, mainly for events, because frequent use can damage and break brow hair, suggesting waxing between sessions for hold without chemicals. [1][2]

Medical News Today lists other ways to shape or fill the brows, including brow gels, tinting and pencil for non-permanent options, and microblading, nanoblading, microshading and tattooing for semi-permanent ones; it describes lamination as more affordable than microblading. [1] New Beauty names microblading and tinting as other semi-permanent options. [2]
The effect on appearance, a fuller, more uniform and upswept brow, is described by practitioners and users [1]. It has not been quantified in published trials.

Reported duration varies between sources, from two to six weeks in New Beauty to six to eight weeks in Medical News Today, with water exposure, lifestyle and the brow growth cycle cited as influences. [1][2] Over-processing, with the solution left on too long, is described in New Beauty as capable of leaving hair frizzy and brittle. [2]

The 2025 review reports that ammonium thioglycolate and thioglycolic acid are hydrophilic and can be absorbed through skin by intracellular and transappendageal routes, and that they can cause allergic contact dermatitis with irritation, dryness and erythema. The authors also discuss effects on hair shape, structure and pigmentation and describe possible systemic effects involving reproductive, ocular, respiratory and endocrine systems, while stating that further studies are needed [4].

An optometry clinical report on cosmetic eye enhancements describes chemical irritation and injury risks from products used near the eyes, and a case report describes allergic dermatitis and periorbital swelling after permanent eyelash dye. Experts quoted in such commentary advise patch testing and describe at-home use as higher risk than professional use [5][8].

Medical News Today lists redness, itching, dryness, peeling and bumps among side effects, notes that brows may become dry or prone to breakage, and says product getting into the eyes can cause serious damage. It suggests people with sensitive skin, eczema, contact dermatitis or rosacea check with a dermatologist first, and gives aftercare advice such as keeping brows dry for 24 hours [1].

Practitioners and dermatologists quoted in beauty media differ in emphasis. Brow artist Giselle Soto says irritation should not be a problem when the treatment is done properly [3]. Aesthetician Mary Schook says ammonium thioglycolate can weaken hair and cause breakage, and dermatologist Nava Greenfield advises an abundance of caution near the eyes [3]. Dermatologist Karan Lal says prolonged irritation could, in the worst case, cause permanent hair loss and recommends asking for a patch test [2]. Nylon also reports that ingredient disclosure is not required for professional salon products under an FDA labeling exemption and that the FDA has not evaluated the treatment [3].
Lamination is discussed as a way to give brows a groomed, upswept look without makeup. Consumer discussion in beauty forums includes questions about doing it at home [9].

Home kits sell at much lower prices than salon visits, and beauty-forum participants ask whether it is possible to do the treatment at home. [9] The articles above describe only professional treatments, and several experts quoted recommend patch testing and licensed practitioners. [1][2][3]
No studies found that test brow lamination for appearance outcomes. A 2025 review summarises toxicological and dermatological data on the thioglycolate ingredients used in the technique [4].
